name: The Eddington Eclipse Experiment
statement: During a solar eclipse, starlight was seen to bend around the Sun by just the amount Einstein's gravity predicted.
statementAccent: bend around the Sun by just the amount Einstein's gravity predicted
meaning: The Eddington eclipse experiment was the pair of astronomical expeditions of 29 May 1919, organized by Frank Watson Dyson and Arthur Eddington, that tested Einstein's general theory of relativity by measuring how much the Sun's gravity bends the light of distant stars. General relativity predicts that a massive body warps the space around it, so light passing near the Sun should be deflected, shifting the apparent positions of stars seen close to it in the sky. This can only be observed during a total solar eclipse, when the Moon blocks the Sun's glare and stars near its edge become visible. Two expeditions observed the 1919 eclipse, one at Sobral in Brazil and one, with Eddington himself, at the island of Príncipe off West Africa, photographing stars of the Hyades cluster near the eclipsed Sun and comparing their positions with photographs of the same stars taken at night. Newtonian physics predicted a small deflection of about zero point eight-seven arcseconds, while Einstein's general relativity predicted about twice as much, one point seven-five arcseconds. The measured deflection matched Einstein's prediction, confirming general relativity. Announced in November 1919, the result made Einstein world-famous overnight, though the reliability of the data has since been debated.
mechanism: The experiment tested general relativity by comparing the apparent positions of stars near the Sun with their true positions. According to general relativity, the Sun's mass curves the surrounding spacetime, so a ray of starlight grazing the Sun is bent, making the star appear shifted slightly away from the Sun's edge. The size of this shift is largest for stars whose light passes closest to the Sun and falls off with distance. To see stars so near the Sun, the astronomers needed the darkness of a total solar eclipse. During the eclipse of 29 May 1919 they photographed the field of stars, including the bright Hyades cluster, surrounding the blacked-out Sun. They then compared these eclipse photographs with reference photographs of the same star field taken months earlier at night, when the Sun was elsewhere, to measure how far each star's image had shifted. The predicted deflection at the Sun's edge was about zero point eight-seven arcseconds under Newtonian gravity and about one point seven-five arcseconds, twice as large, under general relativity. The measured shifts, chiefly from the Sobral backup telescope and the Príncipe plates, came out near the Einstein value and clearly larger than the Newtonian one, confirming the relativistic prediction.

examples.text: One expedition observed the eclipse at Sobral in Brazil and another, with Eddington, at Príncipe off West Africa on 29 May 1919.
Newton's gravity predicted about zero point eight-seven arcseconds of deflection, Einstein's about one point seven-five, and the measurements matched Einstein.
The result, announced in November 1919, confirmed general relativity and made Einstein world-famous almost overnight.

variants.name: The Einstein prediction
variants.text: The larger deflection of about one point seven-five arcseconds predicted by general relativity, which the measurements confirmed.

whyItMatters: The Eddington eclipse experiment is one of the most celebrated tests in the history of physics, because it provided the first major observational confirmation of Einstein's general theory of relativity. By measuring that starlight passing near the Sun was deflected by about the amount general relativity predicted, roughly twice the Newtonian value, it gave dramatic evidence that gravity is the curvature of spacetime and that Newton's theory, though excellent, is not the last word. The announcement in November 1919 was a landmark public event that made Einstein an international celebrity and general relativity a household phrase, marking a shift in the scientific worldview. The experiment also stands as a classic case study in the philosophy and sociology of science, illustrating how a bold theoretical prediction can be tested against a rival, how difficult measurements are weighed, and how scientific claims are debated and refined; later scrutiny of the 1919 data and its error bars, and modern reanalyses, have become part of that story.

working.text: use the darkness of a total solar eclipse to photograph stars whose light grazes the Sun.
measure how far the stars appear shifted against reference photographs taken when the Sun was elsewhere.
find the deflection near one point seven-five arcseconds, twice the Newtonian value, confirming general relativity.

limits: The Eddington eclipse experiment was a genuine confirmation of general relativity, but its data quality and analysis have been the subject of real historical debate that should be represented honestly. The main telescope at Sobral produced blurred, defocused images, apparently from the Sun's heat distorting the instrument, and this dataset, whose deflection came out closer to the Newtonian value, was discarded from the final conclusion; critics from the 1980s onward argued that Eddington may have selectively excluded data favouring Einstein and that the 1919 error bars were large relative to the effect. However, modern reanalyses of the surviving plates by Dyson, Kennefick, and others generally vindicate the original conclusion, finding a real instrumental problem that justified excluding the blurred plates. The Newtonian prediction is variously given as about zero point eight-three to zero point eight-seven arcseconds.
misreadings: The Eddington eclipse experiment was not a flawless, uncontested measurement; the blurred Sobral main-telescope plates were discarded, and historians have debated whether the exclusion was justified and whether the error bars were too large. It did not disprove Newton's theory outright but showed light bends by about twice the Newtonian amount, matching Einstein. And its conclusion has not been overturned, since modern reanalyses largely uphold it, so treating the experiment as free of controversy, as simply refuting Newton, or as discredited, misreads a genuine but historically debated confirmation of general relativity.
origin: The pair of expeditions of 29 May 1919 organized by Frank Watson Dyson and Arthur Eddington, to Sobral in Brazil and Príncipe off West Africa, whose measurement of starlight bending near the Sun confirmed Einstein's general relativity.
